web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Products, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
question: What does this company sell, to whom, and how much of its revenue rests on one molecule and one supplier country?

epigraph.quote: Our revenue from operations depends on one product i.e. “R-32”.
epigraph.author: Stallion Red Herring Prospectus, risk factors, 11 January 2025 [6]

web_blocks.html: The company describes four product families on its website: equipment and spares for the air-conditioning and refrigeration industry, refrigerants and fluorines, semiconductor and electronics specialty gases, and consumer refrigerants and related products [13]. That list is how management presents the business. The money, however, is concentrated in a few places, and the audited accounts do not show you which.

The audited statement of profit and loss shows revenue from operations as a single line [1]. There is no product-level segment split in the audited notes I checked. The MD&A also labels ₹434.12 crore as revenue from operations, but that figure is total income: audited revenue of ₹430.68 crore plus other income of ₹3.45 crore [2][1]. When a report calls the company a specialty-gas business, check which product is actually generating the money. The mix below comes from the RHP and from management’s remarks, not from the audited notes.

The first family on the website, equipment and spares for air-conditioning and refrigeration, does not show up in the filed numbers. The RHP concentration figures do not separate it, and the sources I read give it no share of revenue. Treat it as part of the company’s shop window rather than as a measured earnings line.

web_blocks.takeaway: Each row points the same way. Refrigerant gases are the bulk of product sales, the company depends on imports for most of its input cost, and ten customers account for three-quarters of revenue. The source is the RHP risk-factor section [6][25].

web_blocks.title: R-32: the product that carries the company

web_blocks.html: R-32 is a refrigerant used in air conditioners. The RHP says the company’s revenue depends on it, in plain terms, and that any fall in demand for it could hurt sales, earnings and cash flow [6]. That is the single biggest concentration in the business. The company’s plan is to make some of it rather than only buy and blend it. The August 2026 call put the planned Bhilwara R-32 plant at 10,000 metric tons, and management described the plant as the first major backward integration [8][2].

The plant has a cash-flow effect that management has tied to a number. An analyst asked on the August call whether the FY27 contribution of about ₹250 crore from the new plant still held, and management answered, “It would change a little bit” [9]. Management also said that the full-year utilisation of about ₹500 to ₹600 crore from the plant still stood for FY28 [9]. Those are management figures for a plant that has not yet started, so treat them as targets that the next two quarters will test.

web_blocks.html: A product map is only useful if you can tie each line to a site and a status. The table does that, using the FY26 annual report and the August 2026 call. Where the two disagree, the takeaway says so.

web_blocks.takeaway: Two entries carry a disagreement you should keep. The HFO plant is about ₹200 crore in the annual report and ₹350 to ₹400 crore on the August call. The Bhilwara R-32 target moved from July 2026 in October 2025 to December 2026 in August 2026. Neither is a reason to reject the plan. Both are reasons to check the next filing.

web_blocks.html: The product map matters most for margin, and management gave its own split on the August call. About half the business is still core business, which management described as lower margin. The other half is the newer business, which it said runs at about a 24% PAT margin [9]. An analyst put the conventional business at about 10% PAT, and management answered yes [9]. The company’s case is that the newer half will lift the average as it grows. That is a forecast for plants that are not yet running, and the filings will show whether the mix moves when the plants do.

Put the two sources of margin side by side. The core business is about half the total and runs at a lower margin, while the newer half is management’s claim of about 24%. If the newer half is about half the business today, the average margin depends on whether that half grows and on whether the plants arrive. Refrigerant gas was 81.85% of product sales in FY24 [25], so the core line is still doing most of the work today.

web_blocks.title: How the business works, end to end

web_blocks.html: The chain is simple to describe. The company buys its raw material, much of it imported, then debulks, blends, bottles and sells refrigerant gases to air-conditioning and refrigeration customers. The planned plants move one step further up the chain. Instead of buying and blending R-32 and HFO, the company would make them. Each step up should earn more per kilogram if it works. That is the thesis behind the capital spending examined in chapter 3.

web_blocks.title: What the filings do not split

web_blocks.html: No filed number gives the revenue of the helium project, of R-32, or of the distribution business on its own. The audited revenue line is one figure, and the RHP gives broad percentages. For the new lines, the only numbers are management’s, and they describe plants that are not yet running. Use them as targets, and check each one against the next quarterly result.

web_blocks.title: Helium: the second product family, and a different supply chain

web_blocks.html: The Khalapur facility is the company’s helium project. Management described an installed capacity of 1,200 metric tons a year and said it expected commercial operations to begin in the coming quarter, as of August 2026 [9]. Liquid helium is sourced under a partnership with Sharjah Oxygen Company in Dubai, which sources from RAS Gases & Oilfields in Qatar [1]. On the same call, asked about the outlook, management said: “The next two three years Helium outlook is shortfall and higher …” [8]. That is management’s own forecast, and chapter 4 sets it against independent data. On the same call management said it expected the plant to be used at about 20% of its 1,200 metric tons next year, not 50%, and that the ramp would be gradual [9]. It agreed with an analyst that the helium rate had risen sharply and was now roughly stable near ₹4,000 a kilogram [9]. Capacity is not output, and the sources give no date for full use.

Helium is a different kind of business from refrigerant gas. In October 2025 management explained that helium is not manufactured by anyone. It is recovered as a by-product, then refined and liquefied, and the company’s role is in processing and handling [11]. That makes the helium project a logistics and purification business whose inputs depend on a few producing countries, which is the point the next chapter tests.

The helium supply link runs through a partnership with Sharjah Oxygen Company in Dubai, which sources liquid helium from RAS Gases & Oilfields in Qatar. The annual report calls it a long-term strategic partnership [1]. The contract terms are not in the sources, so I cannot say how long it runs or what share of supply it covers. That is the first thing to ask about any helium revenue number.

web_blocks.title: Customers and the cost of concentration

web_blocks.html: Ten customers accounted for 77.32% of revenue in the six months to September 2024, against 72.88% in FY22 [6]. The top two customers alone were 35.34% of revenue in FY24 [6]. Concentration of that size is not unusual in industrial supply, but it changes what a lost order means. A single large customer taking volume elsewhere moves the whole revenue line, not a slice of it.

The top-ten share has risen in every period the RHP reports, from 72.88% in FY22 to 74.77% in FY23, 75.69% in FY24 and 77.32% in the six months to September 2024 [6]. That can be normal for an industrial supplier, but it means the business is more exposed to its largest buyers each year. That is the direction to watch.

The arithmetic of the top two is blunt. In the six months to September 2024 the top two customers were 30.66% of revenue and the top ten 77.32% [6]. That leaves about 23% of revenue for every other buyer combined. A decision by one of the top two to cut volume or move a contract would reach about a third of the company’s sales in one move. The sources I checked do not give the length of those relationships.

Put the chapter in one sentence. The company sells mainly refrigerant gas, buys most of its input from abroad, depends on a small group of buyers, and is building plants to make its main product rather than only buy it. Each feature is in the filings, and each one means the margin history matters more than the revenue growth.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Ask yourself which part of this business you would own if the company disappeared tomorrow. The answer is R-32 distribution and blending, a helium project still being commissioned, and a customer list that is heavily concentrated. Each of those is a real asset, and each is a different risk. The mix matters more than the total, so keep the product map in view as you read the margin chapters.

A caution about the sources. Management describes the business in broad strokes, and the RHP gives the cleanest percentages. Where the two disagree, I have used the filed document and labelled the management remark as a remark.

book_paragraphs: Let me describe what the company sells, because the words on the website are broader than the money. There are four product families: equipment and spares for air conditioning and refrigeration, refrigerants and fluorines, semiconductor and specialty gases, and consumer refrigerants. That is a wide shop window. But when you look at the filed numbers, refrigerant gases are the bulk of product sales. In the six months to September 2024 they were about 87 percent of product revenue.

The most important thing in this chapter is one sentence from the Red Herring Prospectus. The company said plainly that its revenue depends on one product, R-32. R-32 is a refrigerant used in air conditioners. If demand for it falls, or the company loses its position in it, the business has very little else to fall back on. That is the reason the planned plant at Bhilwara matters. The company wants to make R-32 rather than only buy, debulk and blend it.

The audited statements do not split revenue by product, and that is worth knowing. The revenue line is a single line in the notes. So when someone tells you what share of profit comes from helium or from the new plant, ask them where the number comes from. In this report I have used the RHP and the transcripts, and I have labelled each figure with its source.

The helium project at Khalapur is a different kind of business. Management says the facility has an installed capacity of 1,200 metric tons a year and expects to start commercial operations in the coming quarter. Helium is not manufactured by anyone. It is recovered as a by-product, then refined and liquefied. So the company is a purifier and handler, not an owner of a resource, and its supply depends on a few producing countries. Management itself forecast a helium shortfall over the next two or three years, with a tighter market. Treat that as their forecast, and test it against the independent data in chapter 4.

Customer concentration is the other half of the picture. Ten customers made up about three-quarters of revenue in the six months to September 2024. The top two were about 35 percent of revenue in FY24. In a business like this, a large customer is a relationship that matters, and a lost order moves the whole revenue line. You want to know how that concentration is changing over time, and the next filing will tell you.

Now look at the plant map, because a product map is only useful when you can tie each line to a site and a status. The annual report lists four operating plants: Khalapur, Ghiloth, Manesar and Panvel. It also lists two plants under construction, at Mambattu and at Khalapur. The helium unit is at Khalapur. Bhilwara is different again. It is the planned 10,000 tonne R-32 plant, and the annual report says development began during the year. Keep those three names separate, because the filings describe them in slightly different ways.

Two timelines in the record do not match. The October 2025 call promised Bhilwara within nine months, which meant July 2026. The August 2026 call moved the target to the end of December 2026. The HFO plant has a different problem. The annual report puts it at about 200 crore, while management put the capex at 350 to 400 crore in August. I have not resolved that gap, and I say so rather than pick the number I like.

Management’s own split of the business is the most useful margin clue you have. On the August call management said about half the business is still core business at a lower margin, and the newer half runs at about a 24 percent PAT margin. An analyst put the conventional business at around 10 percent, and management answered yes. If the newer half grows as planned, the average should rise. That is a forecast for plants that are not yet running, and it is the central promise to test.

The helium numbers deserve the same discipline. Management said that next year the Khalapur plant would be used at about 20 percent of its 1,200 tonne capacity, not 50 percent, and that the ramp would be gradual. Capacity is not output. The company also said the helium rate has risen sharply and is now roughly stable near 4,000 rupees a kilogram. A rate is not revenue, and the sources give no volume for the first full year.

Here is a practical way to hold all of this. Picture the company as three businesses sitting on one balance sheet. The first is a large refrigerant distribution and blending business that earns most of its money today. The second is a planned R-32 plant that, if it works, will change the cost of its main product. The third is a helium and specialty-gas business that is still starting up. Each has its own economics, and the report tests each one separately.

The comparison with peers helps here. The RHP lists SRF, Gujarat Fluorochemicals and Navin Fluorine as the peers it chose [7]. Navin kept the highest PAT margin of the three in FY24. Gujarat Fluorochemicals saw its PAT margin more than halve in a single year. Both facts are useful. One shows that a specialty mix can hold margin. The other shows that even a bigger peer can be cut in half within a year. Stallion sits closer to the second story than the first, which is why its single-product dependence matters so much.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Ask which part of this business you would still own if the refrigerant line stopped growing tomorrow. The honest answer is that the company is most valuable in a case where R-32 keeps working and the new plant arrives on time. That is a narrow path, and it is worth stating in your own words before you read the next chapters.
